title: The Op-Amp Comparator: A Switch That Snaps at the Reference
topic: Open-loop op-amp as a comparator — strip away the feedback resistor and the op-amp's enormous gain forces the output to one of the two supply rails the moment V_in crosses V_ref; the analog input becomes a clean digital decision

beats.narration: An op-amp with no feedback resistor — how does it turn a smooth voltage into a clean digital decision?

elements.content: No feedback — the gain runs wild. Why does that help?

beats.narration: V in goes to the plus input, a fixed reference V ref to the minus input. There is no feedback wire — the op-amp runs open loop, with a gain in the hundreds of thousands.

elements.content: Op-amp triangle with V_in into V+ and V_ref into V-; output line; +V_sat and -V_sat supply rails labelled

beats.narration: The transfer characteristic is brutal. Below V ref the output sits at minus V sat. Above V ref it jumps to plus V sat. The transition is essentially vertical.

elements.content: V_in horizontal axis with V_ref marked; V_out vertical axis from -V_sat to +V_sat
Step function — -V_sat for V_in < V_ref, +V_sat for V_in > V_ref; vertical jump at V_ref

beats.narration: Feed it a triangle wave. Each time the input climbs past V ref, the output snaps high; each time it falls back below, the output snaps low. A smooth analog input becomes a clean square wave.

elements.content: Top scope trace: triangle V_in oscillating around V_ref
Bottom scope trace: square V_out flipping between +V_sat and -V_sat at each V_ref crossing; vertical edges aligned

beats.narration: That is what a comparator does — turn an analog crossing into a digital edge. Zero-crossing detectors, level alarms, every analog-to-digital converter starts here.

elements.content: the bridge from analog to digital — one comparison at a time
